orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the October 29, 2014 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of amended complaint against appellants.

facts.factual_summary: While directing a rehearsal at the art venue, plaintiff’s right foot went off an unguarded walkway edge and she fell into a water-filled trench 15 inches below. The walkway was dark while the stage was lit; appellants controlled railing removal and lighting.

legal_issues.finding: Appellants failed to negate duty: they retained control of railings and lighting and removed the railing.
The court considered appellants’ removal of the railing and conceded design of the condition when rejecting their duty/obviousness grounds; it did not finally adjudicate negligent creation.
Appellants failed to establish both obviousness and absence of inherent danger. Removed railings left adjacent trenches without protection, warning or illumination.

quality.notes: Review scope: a personal fall into a trench is explicit, but no slip or trip is identified. Keep other_fall and null pending human scope review. Private ownership/control and negligence merits are clear. Trench water is destination, not an asserted slippery surface. Director/producer is other, with no employment contract inferred. Prior calibration exposure: submissions/becca/CAL_002.json, NY-2993705; not a fresh blind example.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On April 1, 2010, the plaintiff allegedly was injured while conducting a rehearsal of a play that she was producing and directing at a venue known as the Galapagos Art Space, in a building which was owned by the defendant Brooklake Associates, L.P. Galapagos Art Space was owned by the defendant Galapagos at Dumbo, Inc., and managed by the defendant Two Trees Management Co., LLC (hereinafter collectively the appellants). As the plaintiff was walking toward the stage and giving direction to one of the actors, she fell into a water-filled trench when her right foot went off an unguarded edge of the walkway leading to the stage from the center aisle of the venue. The base of the water-filled trench was situated 15 inches below the walkway. The area where the plaintiff had been walking was dark at the time of the accident, while the stage was lit. This was the first rehearsal of the play at the venue.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants Brooklake Associates, L.P., Two Trees Management Co., LLC, and Galapagos at Dumbo, Inc., appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Toussaint, J.), dated October 29, 2014, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint insofar as asserted against them.

Here, contrary to the appellants' contention, they failed to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the amended complaint insofar as asserted against them on the basis that they did not owe a duty of care to the plaintiff ( see Basso v Miller , 40 NY2d at 241). The evidence submitted by the appellants in support of their motion demonstrated that they retained control over the venue by making the ultimate decision as to whether the railings in the area where the accident occurred would be removed, removing that railing, and controlling the condition of the lighting during the rehearsal. Moreover, the appellants failed to establish, prima facie, that the alleged condition that caused the plaintiff to fall, which they concede was designed by the principal of the corporation that owned the Galapagos Art Space during its construction, was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.

The evidence they submitted demonstrated that, once the railing system was removed from the area where the accident occurred, the trenches next to the stage were left unprotected, without any warnings or illumination around them to warn of the height differential, while the other trenches within the venue were protected by permanent railings
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the appellants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint insofar as asserted against them.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the February 10, 2014 denial.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff was working in defendant’s backyard when coworker Lopez allegedly tripped on a hose and dropped a rock slab onto plaintiff’s hand. Another coworker described Lopez slipping and falling on the hose; plaintiff is not described as falling.

legal_issues.finding: Depositions initially established inability to identify why Lopez fell, but another eyewitness’s affidavit identifying the hose raised a triable issue.

The Monday motion was timely because the deadline fell on Saturday. Lopez’s materially changed errata testimony lacked an explanation and could not be considered; affirmance rests on merits instead of untimeliness.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition did not identify why Lopez tripped.
Lopez’s deposition did not identify cause; his unexplained hose errata was rejected. Another coworker’s eyewitness affidavit raised a factual issue.

quality.notes: Nonfall exclusion concerns the injured plaintiff, not the coworker who fell. no_person_fall encodes that injured-person mismatch. Employment by defendant is not inferred; no Labor Law holding. Substantive causation is addressed, so not procedural-only.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries allegedly sustained while he was working in the backyard of a residence owned by the defendant. The plaintiff alleged that he was injured when a coworker, the nonparty Oscar Lopez, tripped and fell on a garden hose, and dropped a slab of rock onto the plaintiff's hand.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Baisley, Jr., J.), dated February 10, 2014, which denied his motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Contrary to the Supreme Court's conclusion, the defendant's motion for summary judgment was timely. Here, the last day to make the motion for summary judgment fell on a Saturday. Accordingly, the defendant was permitted to file the motion "on the next succeeding business day" (General Construction Law § 25-a [1]; see CPLR 3212 [a]; Rodriguez v Board of Educ. of City of Yonkers , 301 AD2d 641 [2003]). Therefore, the defendant's motion, which was made the following Monday, was timely.

In support of his motion, the defendant submitted, inter alia, a transcript of the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, who testified that he did not know why Lopez tripped. The defendant also submitted a transcript of the deposition testimony of Lopez, who similarly testified that he did not know what caused him to fall. Although Lopez later amended his testimony in a post-deposition errata sheet to reflect that he tripped over a garden hose, he failed to offer any reason for materially altering the [*2] substance of his deposition testimony. Therefore, the amended testimony could not properly be considered

However, in opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing of his entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on this ground, the plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact. The plaintiff submitted an affidavit of another coworker who was present in the backyard and standing next to Lopez at the time of the accident. This coworker stated that Lopez slipped and fell on a garden hose that was laying across the backyard in the area where they were working.

Since the plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact in opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing, the defendant was not entitled to summary judgment on the ground that the plaintiff was unable to identify the cause of his accident
Accordingly, the defendant's motion for summary judgment is denied.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ limited appeal from the September 7, 2010 reargument order.
orders.trial_court_action: Upon reargument vacated prior denial and granted dismissal against the Association.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on wet grass in a common area outside her condominium unit within a subdivision of the Chapel Hill Estates complex on October 10, 2006.

legal_issues.finding: Association established no maintenance duty for the accident area; plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue. The opinion does not specify the documents or allocation underlying that conclusion.

quality.notes: Private condominium common area is expressly within the complex; property_basis other reflects that context without attributing ownership/control to the Association. Resident role other avoids inferring owner versus tenant. Wet grass is other, not a confirmed puddle. Granted reargument involves substantive duty; only the September order is appealed.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order entered September 7, 2010, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff Chaya Rinberg (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) alleged that on October 10, 2006, she slipped and fell on wet grass in a common area located outside of her condominium unit within the Hillside at Chapel Hill, which is one of six subdivisions within the Chapel Hill Estates complex in Peeks-kill.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal, as limited by their brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Bellantoni, J.), entered September 7, 2010, as, upon reargument, in effect, *861 vacated so much of an order of the same court entered March 18, 2010, as denied that branch of the motion of the defendant Chapel Hill Estates Homeowners Association, Inc., which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as assert against it, and thereupon granted that branch of the motion.

The Association established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that it had no duty to maintain the area where the injured plaintiff allegedly fell (see Alvarez v Prospect Hosp., 68 NY2d 320, 324 [1986]; Pulka v Edelman, 40 NY2d 781 [1976]; Delgardio v Davis, 86 AD3d 589 [2011]). In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact

Accordingly, the Supreme Court, upon reargument, in effect, properly vacated so much of its prior order as denied that branch of the Association’s motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it, and thereupon properly granted that branch of the motion.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the July 27, 2020 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow and ice on premises owned by the school-district defendants at about 5:55 a.m. on March 15, 2017. His deposition described snowfall the prior day into overnight hours producing 6–12 inches.

legal_issues.finding: The storm rule deferred remediation until adequate time after cessation; defendants established insufficient time here.
Plaintiffs failed to raise an issue whether defendants created or exacerbated the condition during snow removal; mere failure to remove all accumulation was insufficient under the stated rule.
Plaintiff’s deposition established insufficient time after the snowfall for remediation; plaintiffs raised no triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants relied on plaintiff’s deposition concerning timing and amount of snowfall; no weather records or expert are identified.

quality.notes: Owned premises plus express Union Free School District identity supports public-property exclusion. Specific site use/location and injured role are unstated. Snow-removal methods and exact storm-end time are not supplied. Apply unchanged rules to this 2022 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On March 15, 2017, at approximately 5:55 a.m., the plaintiff David Henenlotter allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on snow and ice on premises owned by the defendants.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (James P. McCormack, J.), entered July 27, 2020. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
David Henenlotter et al., Respondents, v Union Free School District No. 23 et al., Appellants.

Here, in support of their motion, the defendants submitted, inter alia, Henenlotter's deposition testimony, which established, prima facie, that snow began to fall the day before the incident and continued to fall into the overnight hours, producing 6 to 12 inches of snow, and that [*2] the defendants did not have a reasonably sufficient time to ameliorate the hazards caused by the storm

In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Contrary to the plaintiffs' contention, they failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendants either created or exacerbated the condition which allegedly caused Henenlotter to slip and fall
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Denny’s limited appeal from the January 12, 2011 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted dismissal on creation/actual notice grounds but denied it on constructive notice.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow and ice in Denny’s parking lot immediately after leaving his car. He testified that he noticed the ice after falling; the manager described an incomplete inspection primarily for garbage.

legal_issues.finding: Trial court granted defendant relief on this ground; current appeal concerns only the remaining constructive-notice ground, without a fresh appellate merits determination here.
Trial court granted defendant relief on this ground; current appeal concerns only the remaining constructive-notice ground, without a fresh appellate merits determination here.

Plaintiff’s failure to see ice beforehand did not prove invisibility. Routine inspections did not establish recent formation; the manager had not inspected the entire lot for ice, and her later contradictory affidavit created a credibility issue.
Manager’s later affidavit was tailored to avoid her deposition testimony; the conflict raised credibility for trial.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described seeing ice after falling; Denny’s manager gave deposition testimony and a later conflicting affidavit.

quality.notes: Restaurant parking lot supports private control without inferred ownership. Partial relief below is not a mixed appellate outcome: the entire appealed portion is affirmed. No customer role, exact date, storm or recurring-condition finding inferred.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ORDERED that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Plaintiff commenced this action alleging that he slipped and fell on snow and ice in the parking lot of defendant Denny’s, Inc., also, as noted by Supreme Court, improperly sued as Denny’s Restaurant (Denny’s).

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Donna M. Siwek, J.), entered January 12, 2011 in a personal injury action. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied in part the motion of defendants for summary judgment.

As relevant to this appeal, the court granted the motion in part with respect to Denny’s, determining that Denny’s was entitled to summary judgment insofar as the second amended complaint, as amplified by the bill of particulars, alleged that Denny’s was negligent in creating the icy condition and in having actual notice of it, but that Denny’s failed to meet its initial burden on the motion of establishing as a matter of law that it lacked constructive notice of the icy condition. Denny’s appeals, contending that the court should have granted the motion in its entirety with respect to it. We affirm.

Contrary to Denny’s contention, the fact that plaintiff did not -2- 110 CA 11-01559 notice the ice before he slipped on it does not establish Denny’s entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the issue whether the ice was visible and apparent. Indeed, plaintiff testified without contradiction at his deposition that he observed the ice after he fell, immediately after he exited his car

Contrary to Denny’s further contention, the deposition testimony of Denny’s manager that she routinely inspected the parking lot did not establish as a matter of law that the ice formed so close in time to the accident that Denny’s may not be charged with constructive notice of it (see Conklin v Ulm, 41 AD3d 1290). The manager acknowledged at her deposition that she did not inspect the entire parking lot on the morning in question, and that she was primarily looking for garbage, not icy conditions.

Although the manager later set forth in an affidavit that she specifically inspected the parking lot for icy conditions when she left the restaurant for the bank at 9:00 A.M., that assertion is at odds with her deposition testimony. We thus conclude that the affidavit was “ ‘tailored to avoid the consequences of’ ” that deposition testimony (Tronolone v Jankowski, 74 AD3d 1721, 1722), and that the conflict between her deposition testimony and her affidavit raises a question of credibility to be resolved at trial (see Palmer v Horton, 66 AD3d 1433, 1434).
